analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all funding for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
analysis.headline: The bill would zero out the CFPB's funding; it was introduced with 6 Republican cosponsors and has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since January 2025 with no action or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) to cap the agency's funding at $0, which would shut down its operations [S2][S3]. The CFPB was created after the 2008 financial crisis to police banks, credit card issuers, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies, and it has the power to write rules, investigate, and return money to consumers who were cheated. Wiping out its funding would end that oversight for banks and nonbank financial companies alike. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies would benefit, because the agency that writes and enforces consumer financial rules would have no money to operate. Financial companies would no longer face CFPB investigations, enforcement actions, or rules that carry financial penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the CFPB's funding at $0 by amending the section of the 2010 law that sets the Bureau's budget, effectively shutting down the agency's operations.
Removes the CFPB's budget authority entirely by striking the provisions that previously set the Bureau's funding level and adjusted it for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers would bear the cost. Without a funded CFPB, there would be no federal agency policing credit card fees and interest rates, payday loan terms, debt collection abuses, or errors in credit reports, and consumers who were harmed would lose the agency that returns money through enforcement actions.

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave no funded federal watchdog for consumer financial products, ending the CFPB's ability to police lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies and to return money to consumers through enforcement.

Supporters of the CFPB's current structure argue its funding from the Federal Reserve rather than annual appropriations was deliberately designed to insulate the agency from industry pressure; the bill removes that insulation by instead limiting funding by statute, which supporters of the bill would call accountability and critics would call a standing invitation to defund oversight in every future Congress. The bill would also eliminate oversight of nonbank lenders, who were outside other regulators' reach before the CFPB existed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear benefit to financial companies — freedom from the agency that regulates them — and a clear cost to consumers, who lose the cop on the beat for loans, credit cards, debt collection, and credit reports. There is no provision in the bill that transfers the CFPB's work to another agency, so the cost side is a straightforward loss of enforcement, not a restructuring.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has gotten no further action — no hearing, no vote, no movement.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the Defund the CFPB Act on January 29, 2025, with six Republican cosponsors: Sens. Barrasso, Scott of Florida, Daines, Blackburn, Rounds, and Lee.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill caps funding of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau at $0.
No further action has been taken on the bill since the committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained because nothing has happened — the CFPB's funding authority is unchanged and the bill has not advanced. If the bill never moves, the beneficiaries would be banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies, which would keep an agency with no budget from writing rules or bringing enforcement actions against them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — the bill has gone nowhere

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to cap CFPB funding at $0.

sides.party_line_note: All seven senators behind the bill are Republicans; no Democrat or Independent has cosponsored it, and no votes have been held.

industries.note: A zero-funded CFPB cannot write rules on overdraft fees, credit card late fees, or account practices, or bring enforcement actions against banks. Consumers lose the regulator that polices these fees and returns money through enforcement.
Payday and other nonbank lenders are outside the reach of traditional bank regulators; the CFPB was the main federal agency overseeing their loan terms. Shutting it down removes that oversight.
Debt collection is one of the CFPB's most-active complaint and enforcement areas. Without funding, the agency cannot process complaints or sue collectors over abusive practices.
The CFPB supervises the credit bureaus and handles consumer disputes over credit report errors. A defunded bureau leaves consumers with weaker recourse when reports contain mistakes.

industries.industry: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (federal consumer watchdog)
industries.note: The bill would eliminate the agency's entire operating budget, ending its rulemaking, supervision, complaint handling, and enforcement functions.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has received no committee action since referral in January 2025. Standalone bills to abolish or defund the CFPB have historically stalled in committee even when their sponsors' party controls the chamber; the likelier path, if any, is that the idea resurfaces as an amendment to a broader financial or spending bill rather than advancing on its own.
